title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 31
paragraphs: Having descended the hill, the general Pierre was chasing turned sharply to the left, and Pierre, losing sight of him, galloped into ranks of infantry marching ahead. He tried to pass them on the right or the left, but soldiers were everywhere, all with the same preoccupied expressions, busy with some unseen but clearly important task. They all stared with dissatisfied, questioning looks at this heavyset man in a white hat who, for some unknown reason, threatened to trample them under his horse's hooves.
"Why are you riding into the middle of the battalion?" one of them shouted at him.
Another poked his horse with the butt of a musket, and Pierre, leaning over his saddlebow and barely able to control his shying horse, galloped ahead of the soldiers to an open space.

There was a bridge ahead, where other soldiers stood firing. Pierre rode up to them. Without realizing it, he had reached the bridge across the Kolocha between Gorki and Borodino, which the French — having occupied Borodino — were attacking in the first phase of the battle. Pierre saw that there was a bridge in front of him and that soldiers were doing something on both sides of it and in the meadow, among the rows of freshly mown hay he hadn't noticed through the campfire smoke the day before; but despite the incessant firing, he had no idea this was the actual battlefield. He didn't notice the bullets whistling from every side or the projectiles flying over him, didn't see the enemy on the other side of the river, and for a long time didn't notice the killed and wounded, though many fell near him. He looked about him with a smile that never left his face.
"Why is that fellow in front of the line?" somebody shouted at him again.
"To the left! Keep to the right!" men shouted at him.
Pierre went to the right and unexpectedly ran into one of Raevsky's adjutants, whom he knew. The adjutant looked angrily at him, clearly about to shout, but recognizing Pierre he simply nodded.
"How did you get here?" he said, and galloped on.
Pierre, feeling out of place, with nothing to do, and afraid of getting in someone's way again, galloped after the adjutant.
"What's happening here? May I come with you?" he asked.
"One moment, one moment!" the adjutant replied, and riding up to a stout colonel standing in the meadow, delivered some message, then turned to Pierre.
"Why have you come here, Count?" he asked with a smile. "Still curious?"
"Yes, yes," Pierre agreed.
But the adjutant turned his horse and rode on.
"It's tolerable here," he said, "but on the left flank with Bagration, they're taking a frightful pounding."
"Really?" said Pierre. "Where is that?"
"Come along with me to our knoll. We can get a view from there, and at our battery it's still bearable," said the adjutant. "Will you come?"
"Yes, I'll come with you," Pierre replied, looking around for his groom.

It was only now that he noticed wounded men staggering along or being carried on stretchers. In the very meadow he had ridden across the day before, a soldier lay sprawled across the rows of sweet-smelling hay, his head thrown awkwardly back, his cap fallen off.
"Why haven't they carried him away?" Pierre was about to ask, but seeing the grim expression on the adjutant's face as he too looked that way, Pierre held his tongue.
Pierre couldn't find his groom and rode along the hollow with the adjutant toward Raevsky's Redoubt. His horse lagged behind the adjutant's and jolted him at every step.
"You don't seem very used to riding, Count," the adjutant remarked.
"No, it's not that — her gait just seems so jerky," Pierre said in a puzzled tone.
"She's been wounded!" said the adjutant. "In the left foreleg above the knee. A bullet, no doubt. Congratulations, Count — your baptism of fire!"

Having ridden through smoke past the Sixth Corps, behind the artillery that had been moved forward and was firing — deafening them with its roar — they came to a small wood. There it was cool and quiet, with the smell of autumn. Pierre and the adjutant dismounted and walked up the hill on foot.
"Is the general here?" the adjutant asked on reaching the knoll.
"He was here a minute ago but just went that way," someone told him, pointing to the right.
The adjutant looked at Pierre, as if unsure what to do with him now.
"Don't worry about me," said Pierre. "I'll go up onto the knoll if I may."
"Yes, do. You'll see everything from there and it's less dangerous. I'll come for you."
Pierre went to the battery and the adjutant rode on. They never met again, and only much later did Pierre learn that the adjutant had lost an arm that day.

The knoll Pierre climbed was the famous one later known to the Russians as the Knoll Battery or Raevsky's Redoubt, and to the French as the great redoubt, the fatal redoubt, the redoubt of the center — around which tens of thousands fell, and which the French considered the key to the entire position.
This redoubt consisted of a knoll with trenches dug on three sides. Within the earthworks stood ten guns being fired through openings in the walls.

On both sides of the knoll stood other guns, also firing without pause. A little behind the guns stood infantry. Climbing the knoll, Pierre had no idea that this spot — with its small trenches and handful of guns firing away — was the most critical point of the entire battle.
On the contrary, just because he happened to be there, he thought it one of the least significant parts of the field.

Having reached the knoll, Pierre sat down at one end of the trench surrounding the battery and watched what was happening around him with an unconsciously happy smile. Now and then he stood up and walked about the battery, still smiling, trying not to get in the way of the soldiers who were loading, hauling guns, and constantly running past him with bags and charges. The guns were firing continuously, one after another, with a deafening roar that enveloped the entire area in powder smoke.

In contrast to the dread felt by the infantrymen positioned in support behind them, here in the battery — where a small group of men busy at their work were separated from everyone else by a trench — there was a shared, almost family-like feeling of excitement.

Pierre's unmilitary figure in a white hat made an unfavorable impression at first. The soldiers looked at him sideways with surprise and even alarm as they passed. The senior artillery officer, a tall, long-legged, pockmarked man, moved over to Pierre as if to check the aim of the farthest gun, and studied him with curiosity.
A young round-faced officer, practically a boy, clearly fresh out of the Cadet College and zealously commanding the two guns assigned to him, addressed Pierre sternly.
"Sir," he said, "please step aside. You must not be here."

The soldiers shook their heads disapprovingly at Pierre. But when they had satisfied themselves that this man in the white hat was doing no harm — either sitting quietly on the trench slope with a shy smile, or politely stepping aside for the soldiers as he strolled up and down the battery under fire as calmly as if walking on a boulevard — their hostile distrust gradually turned into a warm, teasing affection, like the kind soldiers feel for their dogs, roosters, goats, and other animals that live with the regiment. They quickly adopted Pierre into their family, gave him a nickname — "our gentleman" — and made fond fun of him among themselves.
A shell tore up the earth two paces from Pierre, and he looked around with a smile as he brushed the dirt it had thrown up from his clothes.
"How is it you're not afraid, sir — really?" a red-faced, broad-shouldered soldier asked Pierre with a grin that showed a set of strong white teeth.
"Are you afraid, then?" said Pierre.
"What do you expect?" the soldier answered. "She's got no mercy! When she comes sputtering down — out go your guts. You can't help being scared," he said, laughing.
Several men with bright, friendly faces stopped beside Pierre. They seemed not to have expected him to talk like a normal person, and the discovery that he did delighted them.
"It's our job as soldiers. But for a gentleman — that's something! There's a real gentleman for you!"
"Back to your posts!" the young officer called to the men gathered around Pierre.
The young officer was clearly performing his duties for the first or second time and therefore treated both his superiors and the men with great precision and formality.

The booming cannonade and rattle of musket fire were growing more intense across the whole field, especially to the left where Bagration's fortifications were, but where Pierre stood the smoke made it nearly impossible to see anything. Besides, his entire attention was absorbed in watching the tight-knit family circle — sealed off from everything else — formed by the men in the battery. His first unconscious surge of joyful excitement from the sights and sounds of the battlefield had now been replaced by a different feeling, especially since he'd seen that soldier lying alone in the hayfield. Now, sitting on the trench slope, he studied the faces around him.

By ten o'clock about twenty men had already been carried away from the battery; two guns were smashed, and cannonballs landed more and more frequently, while spent bullets buzzed and whistled around. But the men in the battery seemed not to notice any of this — cheerful voices and jokes could be heard on all sides.
"A live one!" shouted a man as a whistling shell approached.
"Not this way! Go to the infantry!" added another with loud laughter, watching the shell fly past and fall into the supporting ranks.
"Bowing to a friend, are you?" remarked another, teasing a militiaman who ducked low as a cannonball flew over.
Several soldiers gathered by the trench wall, peering out to see what was happening in front.
"They've pulled back the front line — it's retreated," they said, pointing over the earthwork.
"Mind your own business," an old sergeant shouted at them. "If they've fallen back, it's because there's work for them farther behind."
And the sergeant, grabbing one of the men by the shoulders, shoved him with his knee. This was followed by a burst of laughter.
"To the fifth gun — wheel it up!" came shouts from one side.
"All together now, like bargemen!" came the cheerful voices of the men moving the gun.

"She nearly knocked our gentleman's hat off!" cried the red-faced joker, showing his teeth and teasing Pierre. "Clumsy thing!" he added reproachfully to a cannonball that struck a cannon wheel and a man's leg.
"Come on, you foxes!" said another, laughing at some militiamen who, stooping low, entered the battery to carry away the wounded man.
"Don't like this porridge, do you? Scared crows!" they shouted at the militiamen who stood hesitating before the man whose leg had been torn off.
"Come on, lads... oh, oh!" they mimicked the peasants. "They really don't like it!"
Pierre noticed that after every hit on the redoubt, and after every loss, the liveliness only grew.

Like the flames of a hidden fire leaping more and more vividly from an approaching thundercloud, so — as if in defiance of what was happening — the lightning of an inner fire glowed ever more intensely in the faces of these men.

Pierre didn't look out at the battlefield and didn't care what was happening there; he was entirely absorbed in watching this fire that burned ever more brightly, and he felt it flaming up in the same way in his own soul.

At ten o'clock the infantry that had been in the bushes in front of the battery and along the Kamenka stream retreated. From the battery they could be seen running back past it, carrying their wounded on their muskets. A general and his staff came to the battery, spoke to the colonel, gave Pierre an angry look, and then left, ordering the infantry supports behind the battery to lie flat so as to be less exposed to fire. After this, from among the infantry ranks to the right of the battery came the sound of a drum and shouts of command, and from the battery they could see those infantry ranks moving forward.
Pierre looked over the trench wall and was particularly struck by a pale young officer who, his sword hanging down, was walking backward, glancing around anxiously.

The infantry ranks disappeared into the smoke, but their drawn-out shout and rapid musket fire could still be heard. A few minutes later, crowds of wounded men and stretcher-bearers came back from that direction. Shells began to fall even more frequently on the battery. Several men lay about, not yet removed. Around the cannon, the men moved still more briskly. No one paid attention to Pierre anymore. Once or twice he was shouted at for being in the way. The senior officer strode with big, rapid steps from gun to gun, his face set in a deep frown. The young officer, his face even more flushed, commanded his men with ever greater intensity. The soldiers passed up charges, turned, loaded, and performed their tasks with strained precision. They moved with little springy steps, as though walking on springs.

The storm had come upon them, and in every face the fire Pierre had watched kindle now blazed brightly. Pierre stood beside the commanding officer. The young officer, his hand to his cap, ran up to his superior.
"I have the honor to report, sir, that only eight rounds are left. Should we continue firing?" he asked.
"Grapeshot!" the senior officer shouted, without answering the question, looking over the trench wall.
Suddenly something happened: the young officer gasped and, folding double, sat down on the ground like a bird shot on the wing. Everything became strange, confused, and hazy in Pierre's eyes.

One cannonball after another whistled by, striking the earthwork, a soldier, or a gun. Pierre, who hadn't noticed these sounds before, now heard nothing else. To the right of the battery, soldiers were running and shouting "Hurrah!" — but backward, it seemed to Pierre.

A cannonball struck the very end of the earthwork where he was standing, crumbling the earth; a black ball flashed before his eyes and at the same instant plunged into something. Some militiamen entering the battery ran back.
"All grapeshot!" the officer shouted.
The sergeant ran up to the officer and informed him in a frightened whisper — like a butler telling his master that they've run out of a requested wine at dinner — that there were no more charges.
"The scoundrels! What are they doing?" the officer shouted, turning toward Pierre.
The officer's face was red and sweating, his eyes glittering under his furrowed brow.
"Run to the reserves and bring up the ammunition boxes!" he yelled, angrily avoiding Pierre with his eyes and speaking to his men.
"I'll go," said Pierre.
The officer, without answering, strode to the opposite side.
"Don't fire! Wait!" he shouted.
The man who had been ordered to go for ammunition stumbled against Pierre.
"This is no place for you, sir," he said, and ran down the slope.
Pierre ran after him, avoiding the spot where the young officer sat.

One cannonball, another, and a third flew over him, falling in front, beside, and behind him. Pierre ran down the slope. "Where am I going?" he suddenly asked himself when he was already near the green ammunition wagons. He halted in confusion, not knowing whether to return or go on. Suddenly a terrible blast threw him backward to the ground. At the same instant he was blinded by a great flash of flame, and immediately a deafening roar, a crackling and whistling made his ears ring.

When he came to his senses he was sitting on the ground, leaning on his hands; the ammunition wagons he'd been approaching no longer existed — only charred green boards and rags littered the scorched grass. A horse, trailing fragments of its shaft, galloped past, while another lay on the ground like Pierre, uttering long, piercing cries.
